claims.text: Single-phase bcc refractory high-entropy alloys can undergo a non-monotonic change in thermal conductivity as chemical short-range order develops.
Isolated SRO clusters initially reduce thermal conductivity through increased phonon scattering.
Above a critical percolation threshold, SRO clusters increase thermal conductivity by forming coherent low-scattering pathways.
A random-solid-solution HfNbTaTiZr alloy is single-phase bcc and has phonon scattering dominated by mass disorder under the proposed conditions.
Thermodynamic equilibration at intermediate temperatures can establish SRO in bcc refractory high-entropy alloys.
Equilibration over 800–1200 K will nucleate and grow SRO clusters toward percolation.
Rapid quenching or isothermal holding can stabilize a percolating SRO network without long-range ordering or phase separation.
The alloy can remain single-phase bcc without sigma, HCP, or other secondary-phase precipitation across the proposed operating window.
A connected network of chemically ordered clusters has a lower phonon-scattering potential than isolated SRO clusters or the random matrix.
SRO can create distinct local chemical order in bcc refractory high-entropy alloys.
Percolating ordered domains form a continuous coherent lattice with lower effective mass fluctuation and reduced anharmonicity than the disordered matrix.
Reduced mass fluctuation and anharmonicity along the percolating path increase phonon mean free path and thermal transport.
Serial/parallel mixing models assume additive scattering and therefore cannot represent the proposed topological transport transition.
Thermal conductivity will reach a minimum near the onset of SRO percolation and then increase sharply as connectivity increases.
Standard scattering and serial/parallel mixing models predict a monotonic reduction in thermal conductivity with increasing SRO concentration because of mass variance and interface scattering.

The proposed effect requires a potential-energy surface that supports formation and percolation of coherent SRO within the single-phase bcc stability window without favoring phase separation or long-range order.
Existing cited evidence shows that SRO changes screw and edge dislocation mobility in bcc MoNbTaW.
The cited records do not directly demonstrate SRO-driven thermal-conductivity percolation or characterize the required percolating potential-energy surface.
Correlating APT- or TEM-derived SRO connectivity with thermal-conductivity measurements across controlled thermal histories can test whether a conductivity inflection coincides with percolation.
A monotonic conductivity decrease, or absence of a conductivity inflection correlated with measured percolation, would falsify the proposed transition.
